Learning Objectives
Perform an appropriate workup for total hip arthroplasty in patients with a history of septic
arthritis of the hip.
Review surgical considerations for total hip arthroplasty in patients with post-septic arthritis of
the hip.
Explain the outcomes of total hip arthroplasty in patients with post-septic arthritis of the hip.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
The hip is a common location for septic arthritis in adults and children.

Septic arthritis of the hip may result in irreversible joint destruction and the eventual need for
total hip arthroplasty (THA).

Overview
Septic arthritis, although relatively rare in the general population, is a commonly
encountered orthopaedic diagnosis. Also known as pyogenic or suppurative arthritis,
septic arthritis describes an infection of the joint space. The hip, as well as the knee,
shoulder, elbow, and wrist, are common locations for septic arthritis in adults and
children (Resource 1). In some patients, septic arthritis of the hip may result in
irreversible damage to articular cartilage, even with proper management, which may
result in progressive joint destruction. Such joint destruction often results in the need for
THA to decrease pain and dysfunction and improve the quality of life resulting from post-
septic arthritis of the hip. In addition, if a patient has preexisting arthritis at the time of
native hip infection or the infection cannot be cured via joint-preserving surgical
débridement and antibiotic agents, then hip resection may be indicated. Reimplantation
with THA may be considered if adequate management of the infection is achieved.
Epidemiology
Septic arthritis most commonly occurs in immunocompromised patients and those with prior
joint destruction.
Long-term follow-up studies demonstrate that, even with successful management of native hip
infection, many patients have poor functional outcomes.

Epidemiology
The yearly incidence of septic arthritis in the United States is approximately 8 cases per
100,000 individuals.1 In adults, septic arthritis of the hip often occurs in
immunocompromised patients and those with prior joint destruction. Some studies
suggest that approximately one-quarter to one-half of adults with septic arthritis of the
hip have preexisting joint destruction.2,3 The infection usually results from hematologic

spread from distant sources of infection. Risk factors that increase the risk of septic
arthritis include older age, diabetes mellitus, rheumatoid arthritis, intravenous drug use,
and other causes of immunodeficiency. Septic arthritis of this hip should be managed
quickly after the diagnosis is made, with open or arthroscopic irrigation and
débridement of the hip and antibiotic therapy (Resource 2). If the infection cannot be
eradicated via joint-preserving surgical débridement and antibiotic agents, then more
extensive surgical débridement, such as hip resection or staged THA, may be indicated.
In infants and children, septic arthritis of the hip most often results from hematogenous
seeding of the synovium from other concurrent infectious sources, such as pneumonia
or a skin infection. Septic arthritis also may result from direct extension from an adjacent
metaphyseal osteomyelitis (Resource 3). Similar to adults, prompt diagnosis and surgical
débridement of the infection in combination with antibiotic therapy is the key to
successful management; however, long-term follow-up of children and infants with
septic arthritis of the hip reveals that approximately one-third of patients have mild or
moderate functional impairment, with a subset having severe sequelae and joint
destruction that may not be apparent until months later.4-6
Etiology
Staphylococcus aureus is the most common causative organism of septic hip arthritis.
After the hip joint is colonized with bacteria, an acute inflammatory response occurs.
If the infection persists, the associated high levels of cytokines and reactive oxygen species
from the immune response may lead to joint destruction.

Etiology
A wide range of bacteria can cause septic hip arthritis; however, S aureus most
commonly is the causative organism.7,8 The most likely causative organisms vary
depending on the age of the patient and patient risk factors for infection. Joint infection
can occur via hematogenous spread or via direct inoculation from trauma or surgery.

After the hip joint is colonized with bacteria, an acute inflammatory response occurs. If
the infection persists, the associated high levels of cytokines and reactive oxygen species
from the immune response may lead to joint destruction.1 Early in the infectious
process, inflammatory cytokines, including interleukin-1ß and interleukin-6, are released
into the joint by synovial cells, which activates a systemic inflammatory response that
ultimately results in an influx of additional inflammatory cells into the synovial
membrane.1 Resultant elevated cytokine concentration increases the release of host
matrix metalloproteinases and other collagen-degrading enzymes, which may result in
the destruction of cartilage.1
Natural History
Even if a native hip infection can be eradicated, irreversible loss of joint function occurs in
approximately 25% to 50% of patients.
Septic arthritis that occurs during childhood may result in unique sequelae if a native hip is
infected before skeletal maturity. Such sequelae include dysplasia of the acetabulum or a high
hip dislocation.

Natural History
Septic arthritis of a native hip joint requires urgent surgical management because the
pathogenesis of the disease results in rapid cartilage destruction.1 Patients with acute
infection often are treated via open or arthroscopic débridement of the hip.
Occasionally, the infection does not resolve despite prompt management, or infections
are diagnosed late, resulting in chronic, indolent infection, which is associated with a risk
for débridement failure. Although data are limited, studies suggest that 14% to 46% of
infected joints have recurrent or persistent infection despite initial surgical débridement
and antibiotic therapy.3,9,10 Even if infection can be eradicated, irreversible loss of joint
function occurs in approximately 25% to 50% of patients.3,10
Septic arthritis of the native hip also can occur during childhood, which may result in
unique sequelae if a native hip is infected before skeletal maturity. In a long-term

outcome study on late sequelae of septic arthritis of the hip in infancy and childhood,
Betz et al11 reported on 19 infantile hip infections (infection in patients younger than 3
months) at a mean follow-up of 32 years and on 13 childhood hip infections, with a
mean age of 52 years at follow-up. Despite a relatively high Harris hip functional score
(mean score, 79; range, 51 to100), 63% (n = 12) of the infantile hip infections were
dysplastic or dislocated at follow-up, nine of which were not dysplastic or dislocated at
the time of infection. Of the 13 childhood hip infections, three hips were dislocated, and
seven hips had undergone surgical fusion or fused spontaneously.11
Given the outcomes of septic arthritis of the native hip, hip arthroplasty surgeons may
encounter three unique patient cohorts in evaluating a patient with a diagnosis of septic
arthritis of the native hip.
Active, native hip infection in a patient with preexisting degenerative arthritis and/or
failed eradication of infection despite prior surgical débridement
Patient with degenerative arthritis of the hip secondary to native hip infection that has
resolved
Patient with a symptomatic high hip dislocation secondary to childhood native hip
infection that has resolved
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History and Physical Examination
In evaluating patients with post-septic arthritis of the hip, an understanding of their infectious
history with regard to the hip is important.
Important information to obtain includes the timing of hip infection, results of prior cultures,
surgical treatment history, antibiotic treatment history, current antibiotic treatment (if any),
and other active sources of infection.

Patient History and Physical Examination

A thorough history is particularly important in evaluating patients with post-septic
arthritis of the hip. Similar to all musculoskeletal complaints, surgeons must understand
the location of a patient’s pain, the timing and onset of symptoms, aggravating and
alleviating factors, and attempted nonsurgical management. In addition to
understanding symptoms related to hip pathology, surgeons understand a patient’s
infectious history with regard to the hip. Important information to obtain includes the
timing of hip infection, the results of prior cultures, surgical treatment history, antibiotic
treatment history, current antibiotic treatment (if any), and other active sources of
infection. Lastly, surgeons must obtain a complete medical history to identify any
necessary areas of optimization before potential surgical management.
A detailed physical examination includes assessment of gait and leg lengths. Assessment
of range of motion of the affected hip should be compared with that of the contralateral
hip. A detailed neurovascular examination of the lower extremities should be
performed. Prior surgical incisions about the hip should be noted.
Imaging Studies
Standard radiographs to evaluate hip disorders should include a weight-bearing AP view of the
pelvis and AP and cross-table lateral views of the affected hip.
If concern for persistent infection exists, cross-sectional imaging via MRI of the hip may aid in
evaluation for persistent infection, foci of osteomyelitis, or soft-tissue abscesses.

Imaging Studies
Standard radiographs to evaluate hip disorders include a weight-bearing AP view of the
pelvis and AP and cross-table lateral views of the affected hip. If the patient has a high
hip dislocation, such as in those with a history of infantile native hip infection, biplanar
radiographs of the entire femur may aid in preoperative planning.
If the patient history, physical examination findings, and laboratory findings do not
reveal the presence or absence of active hip infection, cross-sectional imaging via MRI of

the hip with and without intravenous contrast may aid in evaluation for persistent
infection, foci of osteomyelitis, or a soft-tissue abscess about the hip. In patients in
whom MRI is contraindicated, a tagged white blood cell (WBC) count may be considered
to determine if infection is present.
Diagnosis
The most important diagnosis to make in evaluating a patient with post-septic arthritis of the
hip is whether an active hip infection is present.
Serum inflammatory markers and synovial fluid aspiration may aid in determining the
presence or absence of native hip infection.

Diagnosis
The most important diagnosis to make in evaluating a patient with post-septic arthritis of
the hip is whether an active hip infection is present. Unfortunately, no preferred method
exists to confirm the absence or presence of a native hip infection. Classically, diagnosis
of a native hip infection is made in patients with elevated serum C-reactive protein (CRP)
levels and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) who had a synovial fluid aspiration of the
hip that revealed a WBC higher than 50,000/mm3 and a synovial WBC differential with a
neutrophil percentage higher than 75%.1 However, hip arthroplasty procedures rarely
are indicated at the time of initial diagnosis of a native hip infection unless patients have
preexisting end-stage degenerative hip changes. More often, patients present weeks to
months after failed attempts at surgical débridement for native hip infection or present
with symptomatic, end-stage arthritis of the hip years after the resolution of a native hip
infection.
For patients recently diagnosed and treated for a native hip infection, standard workup
to evaluate for persistent infection should include laboratory studies, including a serum
WBC, ESR, and CRP level. In patients without other sources of infection in whom these
laboratory studies are persistently elevated or trend upward despite recent surgical
débridement and antibiotic therapy, the hip likely remains infected. Synovial fluid

aspiration of the hip also may be helpful to evaluate for infection. The synovial fluid
should be sent for culture, cell count, and WBC differential. Surgeons must consider if a
patient is being treated via antibiotic therapy in interpreting the results of these tests
because antibiotic agents likely will affect laboratory values and culture results. Physical
examination findings concerning for persistent hip infection include a persistently
draining incision from prior débridement or a sinus tract.
In patients with symptoms related to end-stage arthritis of the hip and a remote history
of native hip infection, the diagnostic workup should begin with serum ESR and CRP
levels. If these laboratory values are within normal limits, then a persistent hip infection
is unlikely. If ESR and/or CRP level are elevated or clinical suspicion for persistent hip
infection remains, then synovial fluid of the hip should be obtained and sent for culture,
cell count, and WBC differential. MRI of the hip or a tagged WBC count also may be
helpful in patients with an elevated ESR/CRP level who have equivocal synovial fluid
analysis results.
Ultimately, if patients are treated surgically, then multiple deep tissue cultures should be
obtained and sent for analysis at the time of the surgical procedure to diagnose the
presence or absence of infection and guide subsequent antimicrobial therapy, if
indicated.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Active, native hip infection is unlikely to resolve via nonsurgical management.
In patients with end-stage arthritis of the hip secondary to a resolved septic hip, standard
nonsurgical treatment options should be trialed according to published clinical practice
guidelines.
In patients diagnosed with an active hip infection, despite prior antibiotic therapy and surgical
débridement of the hip, infection is unlikely to resolve with nonsurgical management.


Nonsurgical Management
Patients with symptomatic end-stage arthritis of the hip from prior native hip infection in
whom a diagnostic workup indicates that the infection has resolved should be offered
classic nonsurgical treatment options for end-stage hip arthritis. Such treatment options
include activity modifications, gait aids, weight reduction in patients with obesity,
acetaminophen, NSAIDs, and/or corticosteroid injections. Nonsurgical management of
hip arthritis should be guided by the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Osteoarthritis of the
Hip (Resource 4).
Surgical Management
In patients with a native hip infection and preexisting end-stage arthritis in whom infection
eradication failed despite surgical débridement and antibiotic therapy, hip resection and
antibiotic spacer placement with subsequent conversion to THA may be indicated.
In patients in whom a prior hip infection has resolved and nonsurgical management of end-
stage arthritis fails, then primary THA may be indicated.

Surgical Management
If a patient is diagnosed with an active hip infection with end-stage hip arthritis or failed
eradication of the infection despite surgical débridement and antibiotic therapy, then hip
resection and antibiotic spacer placement with subsequent conversion to THA may be
indicated after the infection is managed. Hip resection allows for more extensive
débridement of the infection and removal of any foci of osteomyelitis. The antibiotic
spacer allows for high-dose antibiotic agents to be delivered locally to the site of the
infection and aids in subsequent conversion to a definitive hip prosthesis. Antibiotic
spacers may be articulating or non-articulating. Six weeks of culture-directed antibiotic
therapy is performed in addition to surgical management to aid in eradication of the
infection.

In patients in whom a prior hip infection has resolved and nonsurgical management of
end-stage arthritis fails, then primary THA may be indicated. Because infection is no
longer present, staged hip resection and subsequent conversion to THA is not necessary
in such patients. A femoral osteotomy should be considered in patients with a history of
childhood hip infection and subsequent high hip dislocation.
Indications
Staged management via hip resection and subsequent THA is indicated in patients with a
chronic native hip infection or an acute hip infection who have preexisting, end-stage
degenerative arthritis.
Primary THA is indicated in patients with post-septic arthritis if the diagnostic workup reveals
no active infection and nonsurgical management fails.
Native hip resection and antibiotic spacer placement with subsequent conversion to THA is
indicated in the following patients:
Adult patients with a diagnosis of an acute, native hip infection and preexisting, end-stage
arthritis of the hip.
Adult patients with a diagnosis of a chronic, native hip infection despite prior surgical
débridement and antibiotic therapy.

Indications
Indications for primary THA in patients with post-septic arthritis include diagnostic
workup revealing resolution of the infection and failed nonsurgical management to
alleviate symptoms related to end-stage hip arthritis.
Contraindications
Contraindications to primary THA for post-septic arthritis include active hip infection
Proceed with caution in patients with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, a body mass index
greater than 40 kg/m2, and active tobacco use. Modifiable risk factors should be optimized
before arthroplasty, if possible.


Contraindications
Because of the presence of infection and the potential for sepsis and additional
infectious complications, no true contraindications to hip resection and antibiotic spacer
placement with planned conversion to THA exist. However, in low-demand or
nonambulatory patients, definitive Girdlestone hip resection rather than a two-staged
procedure may be considered to minimize surgical management.
Contraindications to primary THA for post-septic arthritis of the hip are the same as
contraindications for primary THA for other noninfectious indications (Resource 5).
Given that patients with post-septic arthritis have a higher risk for infection after hip
replacement than patients with osteoarthritis, preoperative optimization must be
considered. Contraindications to primary THA include active hip infection.
Techniques/Procedures
Extensive surgical débridement is key to successful eradication of infection in patients
undergoing native hip resection and antibiotic spacer placement for active hip infection.
Antibiotic spacers may be articulating spacers or non-articulating spacers.
High-dose antibiotic-laden cement should be used for the antibiotic spacer.
Patients also are treated via 6 weeks of culture-directed antibiotic agents after hip resection
and spacer placement.
Resolution of infection must be confirmed before converting the antibiotic spacer to THA.
In patients undergoing primary THA for end-stage arthritis secondary to a resolved native hip
infection, standard THA techniques can be used.
Subtrochanteric shortening osteotomy may be necessary during THA in patients with a high
hip dislocation because of childhood hip infection.

Techniques/Procedures
In patients undergoing native hip resection and antibiotic spacer placement for active,
native hip septic arthritis, prior surgical incisions and exposure necessary for conversion

to THA should be considered during the surgical approach. After the hip is exposed, the
femoral head is osteotomized in a routine fashion, similar to that for primary THA. All
potentially infected and necrotic tissue is débrided, and thorough irrigation is
performed. Any foreign bodies or hardware that is present should be removed. Multiple
deep tissue cultures should be sent for analysis to guide antimicrobial therapy.
After irrigation and débridement, the antibiotic spacer is placed. Antibiotic spacers may
be articulating spacers or nonarticulating spacers with antibiotic cement or beads placed
into the resected joint. The author of this lesson prefers to place an articulating spacer
because articulating spacers are associated with improved hip function between first-
and second-stage procedures and facilitate easier conversion to THA as demonstrated
by shorter mean surgical time, less blood loss, and lower transfusion rate during
conversion of the antibiotic spacer to THA.12
Multiple types of articulating spacers have been described, including prefabricated
antibiotic cement spacers. The author of this lesson prefers to use an articulating spacer
fabricated intraoperatively to allow for the use of high-dose antibiotic-laden cement and
to potentially guide antibiotic selection, if necessary, based on preoperative culture
results. High-dose antibiotic cements are described as those containing more than 1.0 g
of antibiotic per 40-g batch of cement.13 Heat-stable antibiotic agents that will remain
effective after being mixed with cement should be selected.14
The femoral canal is then prepared via a broach technique for a stable press fit. With the
preferred approach of the author of this lesson, after the ideal broach size is
determined, a corresponding femoral component is created using high-dose antibiotic
cement and appropriate size mold. While the cement for the femoral component is
curing, attention is shifted to the acetabulum. Acetabular reamers are used to ream the
acetabulum just deep to the subchondral bone to improve cement fixation for the
polyethylene liner, taking care to preserve bone for subsequent conversion to THA. High-
dose antibiotic cement is then prepared, and the polyethylene liner designed for
cementation is cemented into place.
After the cement for the acetabular component has cured, the femoral component is
removed from the mold. The femoral component is then impacted into the femoral

canal to achieve a press fit. Trial reduction is then performed with trial femoral heads to
achieve the ideal leg length, offset, and stability of the hip. The real femoral head is then
impacted onto the stem, and the hip is reduced. Standard closure is performed.
Partial–weight bearing is permitted during the treatment phase of infection. Patients are
treated via 6 weeks of culture-directed antibiotic agents, and their inflammatory markers
(ESR and CRP level) are trended to monitor the response to treatment. After completion
of antibiotic therapy, antibiotic agents are discontinued for at least 2 weeks, and
ESR/CRP level are assessed to ensure stable laboratory values off of antibiotic agents
before conversion to THA.
No consensus definition of infection eradication prior to conversion to THA exists;
however, definitions used in the literature often include persistent normalization of CRP
level off of antibiotic agents;15-18 a healed surgical wound;19 and, in some patients,
negative culture via hip aspiration after at least 2 weeks off of antibiotic agents.20
Often, patients with septic hip arthritis have multiple comorbidities. If modifiable risk
factors for recurrent infection are present (ie, poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, active
tobacco use, body mass index greater than 40 kg/m2), patient optimization before
conversion to THA should be considered. After the infection is determined to be
eradicated and the patient is medically ready for surgical treatment, conversion to THA is
performed via standard revision THA techniques.
For patients undergoing primary THA for end-stage arthritis secondary to resolved native
hip infection, standard THA techniques should be used. Intraoperative cultures should
be obtained, and antibiotic therapy should be initiated if cultures are unexpectedly
positive. In patients with a high hip dislocation secondary to childhood hip infection, a
subtrochanteric shortening osteotomy may be necessary during THA (Resource 6). In
addition, these patients also may have a deficient acetabulum, and structural autograft
may be necessary during acetabular reconstruction.21
Outcomes

Two-stage management of native hip infection with hip resection and antibiotic spacer
placement followed by conversion to THA is effective; however, this approach is associated
with a high complication rate and an approximately 5% to 15% risk for recurrent infection after
final implant placement.
If the native hip infection has resolved and patients undergo primary THA for post-septic
arthritis, then outcomes more closely match those of primary THA for other indications;
however, the infection risk remains slightly elevated.

Outcomes
A two-stage procedure with native hip resection and antibiotic spacer placement
followed by conversion to THA is an effective means for the management of infection or
these difficult cases. However, this treatment technique is not without risk for
complications or continued infection. The literature has demonstrated that patients who
complete the entire two-stage process have a postoperative infection rate after final
prosthesis implantation ranging from 5% to 15%15-20,22-25,37,38 (Table 1); however,
studies have reported that 8% to 14% of patients may require antibiotic spacer exchange
for continued infection before conversion to THA, and approximately 25% of patients
never undergo the second procedure because of persistent infection or
death.15,17,18,20,22 A complication unique to the use of an articulating spacer is
dislocation of the spacer. Articulating antibiotic spacer dislocation has been reported in 0
to 13% of patients who undergo treatment for native hip infection15-20,22-25,37,38 (Table
1).

THA performed for arthritis secondary to prior native hip infection that has resolved is
associated with a complication profile that more closely matches that of primary THA for
osteoarthritis. Such patients have an increased risk for subsequent periprosthetic joint
infection. A review of the literature identified 14 studies that included 168
patients.16,21,23,26-36 The overall infection rate in these patients was approximately
2%16,21,23,26-36 (Table 2). However, most data on this topic is in younger patients who
had childhood infections; therefore, the comorbidity profiles of these patients often are
much more conducive to successful surgical outcomes.
